This is Danza de los Diablos (Diablada). 18th century.
on_screen: Title card: Danza de los Diablos (Diablada) · Bolivia · 18th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the Andean Altiplano, with roots in the Uru civilization's Llama llama dance honoring the deity Tiw.
During the Spanish colonial period, it was influenced by autos sacramentales and the process of Christianization.
The first institutionalized squad, Gran Tradicional y Auténtica Diablada Oruro, was founded in 1904.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance represents the struggle between good and evil.
It is a central feature of the Carnaval de Oruro, the Fiesta de la Candelaria, and the Fiesta de La Tirana.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in two camps: angels and demons.
Dancers execute complex geometric figures like circles and crosses.
The choreography features jumps and sword-play, culminating in the defeat of the devil by Saint Michael.
Watch for Demon jump.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally performed with the siku (panpipe) by Sikuris, modern versions use orchestras.
The music consists of two parts: the March and the Devil's Mecapaqueña.
Listen for the siku, orchestra.
A rhythmic, driving sound featuring panpipes or orchestral brass, characterized by a steady, march-like cadence that transitions into the more complex Mecapaqueña.
